reference.source: Brukner and Khan's Clinical Sports Medicine
clinicalPearls: Caused by deposition of calcium hydroxyapatite crystals within a tendon, most often the supraspinatus of the rotator cuff
May be asymptomatic and found incidentally, or cause a chronic ache during the formative and resting phases
The resorptive phase produces acute, severe, often disabling shoulder pain as the deposit softens and is reabsorbed
Distinct from wear-related degenerative cuff tendinopathy, although the two can coexist
Radiographs and ultrasound readily demonstrate the deposit and help track its evolution
Many deposits resolve spontaneously, so initial management is conservative with analgesia and activity modification
Ultrasound-guided barbotage (needle aspiration and lavage of the calcium) is effective for persistent symptomatic deposits
Extracorporeal shockwave therapy can promote resorption and relieve symptoms in resistant cases
reference.pathophysiology: Calcific tendinitis results from deposition of calcium hydroxyapatite crystals within tendon substance, classically the rotator cuff. The process is described as passing through phases: a precalcific phase, a formative phase in which chalk-like calcium accumulates within fibrocartilaginous metaplastic tissue, a resorptive phase in which the deposit softens to a toothpaste-like consistency and is reabsorbed by a vascular and cellular response, and a post-calcific healing phase. The resorptive phase is associated with the most intense pain, owing to raised intratendinous pressure and surrounding inflammation. Because it is a crystal-deposition process, it is distinct from an overload-related degenerative tendinosis.
additionalDifferentials: Septic arthritis or septic bursitis of the shoulder in an acute severe presentation
additionalInvestigations: Plain radiographs to locate, size and characterise the calcific deposit
Ultrasound to confirm the deposit, assess its consistency and guide intervention
MRI where a cuff tear or other pathology is suspected
Clinical assessment of the disease phase from the symptom pattern
Inflammatory markers if septic arthritis or bursitis is a consideration
redFlags: Fever with a hot, swollen joint suggesting septic arthritis rather than a resorptive flare
Rapidly worsening pain with systemic upset requiring exclusion of infection
Failure to improve, raising suspicion of an alternative diagnosis such as a tear
reference.prognosis: The natural history is often favourable, with many deposits resorbing spontaneously and symptoms settling; barbotage and shockwave help resistant cases, and only a minority require surgery.
pitfalls: Mistaking an intensely painful resorptive flare for septic arthritis, or the reverse
Assuming an incidental calcific deposit is necessarily the cause of a patient's pain
Over-investigating what is often self-limiting disease
Delaying targeted treatment such as barbotage or shockwave in persistent, disabling cases
references: Brukner and Khan's Clinical Sports Medicine
management: Begin with conservative care: analgesia, anti-inflammatory medication, activity modification and physiotherapy, as many deposits resorb spontaneously.
Offer a subacromial corticosteroid injection to control pain, particularly during the acutely painful resorptive phase.
Use ultrasound-guided barbotage (needling and lavage) for symptomatic deposits resistant to conservative treatment.
Consider extracorporeal shockwave therapy for persistent formative-phase deposits.
Reserve arthroscopic surgical removal for deposits refractory to all other measures.
Track the deposit and its evolution with radiographs or ultrasound to guide escalation.
